components.gap: Durrett p. 144, right after Theorem 3.4.1, justifies the non-standard letter chi for a standard normal variable: "to see the logic note that the square of a normal has a chi-squared distribution". The routed notation entry (def:p15-clt-notation, central-limit-theorems.tex 17-54) introduces chi with no rationale and no statement of the chi-squared fact. Supply this justificatory claim and its stated fact on the route.

components.gap: Example 3.4.5 (Durrett p. 145) derives the gain law from the roulette wheel (slots 1-36, eighteen red and eighteen black, two green slots 0 and 00, a $1 bet on a colour); the route states only the resulting law +1 w.p. 18/38, -1 w.p. 20/38 (central-limit-theorems.tex 107-113). Example 3.4.7 (p. 146) says the histogram correction is important when the normal approximation is used for small n and gives its reason: reading P(S16 <= 11) as P(S16 <= 11.5) gives the same answer as reading it as 1 - P(S16 >= 12). The route gives the correction rule (lines 119-126; annex 542-545) without the small-n claim or this justification, and it does not state the source's observation that even at n = 16 the corrected value 0.1974 agrees well with the exact 0.1964. Supply the wheel model and these claims.

components.gap: Durrett p. 151 states why the truncation level is c_n = sqrt(n) loglog n: it must make sum_m P(Y_{n,m} != X_m) <= nP(|X_1| > c_n) -> 0, while the variance of Y_{n,m} should be as small as possible, so the level is kept close to the lowest possible level. The route states the level and its estimates (330-346; annex 1118-1132) but not this justificatory claim. The Remark on p. 152 replaces the hypothesis P(|X_1| > x) = x^{-2} by x^{-alpha}, 0 < alpha < 2, and asserts that S_n/n^{1/alpha} then converges weakly to a limit that is not chi; no routed text states or proves that convergence (normal-domains-of-attraction.tex 220-228 only excludes a normal limit). Supply both.

components.gap: Durrett opens Section 3.4.3 (p. 153) with the claim that, since exp(e^4) = 5.15 x 10^23, the Erdos-Kac result does not apply to most numbers encountered in "everyday life". The routed statement and proof (444-457; annex 115-202) omit this claim about the scale at which the theorem becomes informative. Supply it.

components.gap: The remarks after Theorem 3.4.17 (Durrett p. 157) are absent from the route: the constant 3 is not the best known (van Beek (1972) gets 0.8); the method is credited to Feller with the quotation "our streamlined method yields a remarkably good bound even though it avoids the usual messy numerical calculations"; the hypothesis E|X|^3 < infinity is needed to get the rate n^{-1/2}; Heyde (1967): for 0 < delta < 1, sum_n n^{-1+delta/2} sup_x |F_n(x) - N(x)| < infinity iff E|X|^{2+delta} < infinity; and the pointer to Hall (1982). The route keeps only the n >= 10 reduction and the fair-sign lower-order example (530-531; annex 318-323, 438-448), and the boundary (555-557) names the Heyde remark without stating it. Supply these claims with their attributions.

components.gap: Durrett p. 152 introduces Theorem 3.4.14 as "the last word on convergence to the normal distribution", attributes it to Levy, and describes Gnedenko and Kolmogorov (1954) as "a reference that contains the last word on many results about sums of independent random variables"; neither this boundary (534-558) nor the routed normal-domain chapter states the Levy attribution or these characterizations. The boundary also declares Examples 3.4.5-3.4.13 and the Berry-Esseen presentation supplied although their source claims recorded under C001, C005, C019, C025 and C029 are absent, and it names the Heyde rate equivalence without its content. Supply the attribution and claims so that the declared status is true.
